planting.note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring, setting the crown at the depth it grew previously in moist, humus-rich soil.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, consistently moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where it forms a tidy mound of large, heart-shaped, distinctly wavy-margined leaves in a soft green with a grayish cast on the reverse. Named for hosta taxonomist Dr. Fumio Maekawa and derived from the species Hosta hypoleuca, this selection is valued today less as a standalone landscape plant and more as a breeding parent, having passed its wavy leaf margins and vigor into modern blue hostas such as 'Neptune' and 'Joy Ride.' Pale lavender flowers rise above the foliage on tall scapes in mid to late summer. Established clumps are long-lived and need dividing only every several years when the center becomes congested; watch for slugs, the main pest of hosta foliage.

planting.note: Divide and transplant dormant crowns in early spring, setting the crown at the depth it grew previously in moist, humus-rich soil.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, where it forms a small, distinctly upright clump instead of the low mound typical of most hostas. Bred by Herb Benedict as a fourth-generation seedling from 'Dorset Blue,' Salute carries slightly twisted, powdery-blue leaves held nearly vertical in a habit reminiscent of a miniature 'Krossa Regal,' with the strongest blue coating showing in spring before fading somewhat as summer heat arrives. Near-white flowers appear on scapes in summer, and the compact size and upright silhouette make it useful for edging a path or filling a small shaded gap where a spreading hosta would sprawl. This cultivar is also notable as a parent of the popular blue hosta 'Neptune.' Divide congested clumps in spring and watch for slugs, the primary pest of hosta foliage.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun to partial shade; Dazzler is self-fruitful and sets heavy crops of bright red berries without a male pollinator nearby.

directions: Plant in well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral, average soil in full sun to dappled shade; Dazzler forms a dense, rounded, mounding Chinese holly with glossy, dark green, spiny leaves and a heavier berry set than many named Ilex cornuta selections. Like other Chinese hollies it is parthenocarpic, so a single plant reliably produces a prolific fall-into-winter crop of bright red berries without needing a male nearby, an advantage in smaller residential landscapes where only one shrub is planted. It tolerates clay, drought once established, and the heat and humidity of the Gulf Coast and Southeast, and is generally resistant to verticillium wilt. Use it as a hedge, foundation planting, or berried specimen for winter interest and songbird food; prune lightly in late winter after the berry display fades, since flowers and fruit form on the previous year's wood.

common_name: Squeeze Box Inkberry Holly (Upright Pyramidal Male Pollinator Holly)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Squeeze Box is a male-only Proven Winners introduction grown as an upright accent and as the recommended pollinator for female inkberry cultivars such as 'Gem Box' and 'Strongbox' planted within about 50 feet.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, keeping the shallow root zone consistently moist with a steady layer of mulch. Squeeze Box is the first upright, narrowly pyramidal inkberry selection, forming a dense column of small, glossy dark green leaves that holds its shape with little to no shearing, making it a useful native substitute for dwarf Alberta spruce or narrow boxwood columns in a foundation planting or formal accent. As a male-only selection it never sets berries itself, but planting one within about 50 feet of female inkberry cultivars such as 'Gem Box' or 'Strongbox' ensures reliable pollination and fruit set on those plants. Apply an acid-forming, evergreen-type fertilizer in spring, and avoid letting the soil dry out or become waterlogged for extended periods.

common_name: Red Escort Possumhaw Holly (Male Pollinator Deciduous Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Red Escort is a male-only selection of native possumhaw introduced by nurseryman Bob Simpson and is the pollen donor most widely recommended for heavy-fruiting female selections such as 'Warren's Red' planted within pollinating distance.

directions: Plant in moist to average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, siting it within about 100-150 feet of female possumhaw plants since hollies are dioecious and only pollinated females produce the species' celebrated winter berry display. Red Escort is a male-only selection with a neat, dense, globe-shaped habit and glossy dark green deciduous foliage, grown expressly as a reliable pollen source rather than for berries of its own; it is widely paired with heavy-fruiting females such as 'Warren's Red' to guarantee a good fruit set most years. Like other possumhaws it tolerates seasonally wet bottomland soil as well as average garden conditions and needs little upkeep once established. Prune lightly after bloom in spring if a tighter form is wanted, since it carries no fruit display to protect.

common_name: Linebacker Distylium (Upright Columnar Evergreen Screening Shrub)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Linebacker is an upright, dense, columnar distylium selection bred for screening and hedging, staying considerably narrower than spreading selections like 'Vintage Jade'.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Linebacker grows into a dense, strongly upright, columnar mass of small, glossy leaves that emerge reddish before maturing to rich dark green, giving it a much more formal, narrow silhouette than spreading groundcover-type distylium selections. Like other distyliums it produces inconspicuous, petal-less red-stamened flowers in late winter and tolerates full sun, part shade, heat, humidity, and both wet and dry soil with no serious pest or disease issues and minimal pruning needed to stay tidy. Its tight upright habit and tolerance of hard shearing make it a popular low-maintenance substitute for cherry laurel or Leyland cypress in hedges and screens along property lines. Once established it is notably drought tolerant and deer generally leave it alone.
